nameStory: The name "miniature moneywort" comes from its resemblance to the larger, more common moneywort (also called creeping Jenny), but in a tiny package. Traditional moneywort got its name because people thought its round, coin-shaped leaves looked like money - and this little cousin carries on that family resemblance in miniature form.
description: Miniature moneywort is a delicate, low-growing perennial that forms small mats along the ground. This tiny member of the loosestrife family rarely grows more than 2-3 inches tall, with thread-like stems that creep along moist soil. Its small, rounded leaves and tiny yellow flowers make it easy to overlook, but once you spot it, you'll recognize its charming, diminutive presence. As an introduced species from Asia, it's still quite rare in New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, round to oval leaves about the size of your pinky nail, arranged in pairs along thin, creeping stems. They feel smooth and slightly succulent when gently rubbed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Minuscule yellow flowers with 5 petals, often smaller than a pencil eraser. They sit singly in the leaf joints and are so small you might need to get down close to really see their star-like shape.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that hug the ground, with stems that root at the joints where they touch soil. The whole plant has a delicate, almost moss-like appearance from a distance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thread-thin, smooth stems that feel slightly fleshy and break easily when pinched. They trail along the ground in a sprawling pattern, rarely rising more than an inch or two high.

habitat: Look for miniature moneywort in consistently moist, disturbed soils around pond edges, wet ditches, and marshy areas. It favors spots with little competition from taller plants, often appearing in muddy areas that dry out periodically. In New England, it's most likely to turn up near water features in suburban and urban areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as tiny green mats in wet areas. The small leaves are fresh and bright green, and early flowers may begin appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season, when the tiny yellow blooms are most visible. The plant forms its most extensive mats during warm, wet summer months.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing until frost, with leaves remaining green. Seeds develop and disperse during this time, though they're almost too small to see.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots in colder areas, leaving little trace above ground. In milder winters, some leaves may persist but turn reddish or bronze.

funFact: This plant is so tiny that an entire thriving colony can fit in the palm of your hand, yet it's part of the same plant family as much larger, showier flowers like cyclamen and shooting stars!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with baby's tears or small chickweed species, but miniature moneywort's perfectly round leaves arranged in neat pairs along creeping stems set it apart. Remember: "Moneywort has coin-shaped leaves in pairs" - the round leaves are your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's just a small version of regular moneywort, miniature moneywort is actually a completely different species that originated in Asia. The "moneywort" name family can be confusing since several unrelated plants share variations of this name based on their coin-like leaves.
compareHints: Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth. It's also much rarer than other loosestrifes in New England, lacking the robust, sometimes invasive growth of species like yellow loosestrife or gooseneck loosestrife.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement.
Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.

Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground.
